Infectious Diseases of the PNS

LO 1–6 Tick-borne Spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi

🦠🕷️ Lyme Disease

How boards would word it

"A 9-year-old boy is brought to the office in July because his parents noticed his face looked 'lopsided' this morning. Three weeks ago the family returned from a camping trip in coastal Massachusetts, where he recalls a tick bite on his thigh followed by an expanding red rash that resolved on its own after about two weeks. Today he has drooping of both the right and left sides of his face, with inability to fully close either eye. He denies ear pain, vesicles, or hearing changes. Vital signs are normal, and the remainder of the neurologic exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Lyme disease — early disseminated neuroborreliosis (bilateral facial nerve palsy)
What to look for: a preceding self-resolving annular rash plus outdoor/tick exposure in an endemic season, followed weeks later by bilateral facial palsy, is the classic discriminator — Bell palsy is almost always unilateral, and the absence of vesicles/ear pain argues against Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus).
LO 1 Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Borrelia burgdorferi, a microaerophilic spirochete, is the transmissible causative agent of Lyme borreliosis (Lyme disease / Lyme borreliosis / erythema chronicum migrans / borreliosis). It is transmitted by ixodid ("hard body") ticks — deer ticks — and disease can present with musculoskeletal, dermatologic, cardiac, or neurologic manifestations: facial palsy, meningitis, encephalitis, radiculoneuritis, mononeuropathy multiplex, or polyneuropathy.

Lyme disease is the most commonly reported vector-borne disease in the US, concentrated in the Northeast and upper Midwest. Incidence has been rising over time — most likely from growth of the deer herd and expansion of the tick vector's range, not just better recognition.

  • 1996: 16,461 reported US cases (CDC) → 2002: 23,763 cases → 2023: over 89,000 reported cases
  • 80–90% of cases cluster in 8 states: CT, RI, NY, PA, NJ, DE, MD, WI — though cases are reported in nearly every state
  • Prevalence varies widely by region: national average ~6.2/100,000 (1996) vs. 94.8/100,000 in Connecticut vs. 1,247.5/100,000 in Nantucket County, MA
  • True incidence is likely far higher than CDC-reported figures — by 2014 estimates, actual US cases may have reached ~300,000/yr (~10× the reported rate)

Reservoirs: white-tailed deer and the white-footed mouse (Peromyscus leucopus) — the primary reservoir for B. burgdorferi in the US.

Pathophysiology

Vector: Ixodes spp. ("hard body" ticks) — I. scapularis (deer tick, NE/upper Midwest US) and I. pacificus (western US); I. ricinus transmits B. afzelii/B. garinii in Europe. Peak transmission season is April–October, especially June–August.

The tick's proboscis penetrates the epidermis to reach the dermal blood supply; backward-facing, arrowhead-like thorns lock the tick into the skin. After roughly 24–36 hours of attachment, spirochetes housed in the tick's salivary glands migrate into the surrounding dermal tissue. From there, hematogenous and lymphatic spread is facilitated by B. burgdorferi binding to fibronectin receptors on platelets, vitronectin receptors on endothelial cells, and decorin on collagenous fibers — allowing the spirochete to disseminate well beyond the bite site.

Ixodes tick attaches
→
Feeds ≥ 24–36h
→
Spirochetes: salivary gland → dermis
→
Local proliferation (erythema migrans)
→
Fibronectin/vitronectin/decorin-mediated dissemination
→
Early disseminated disease
→
Late/persistent disease if untreated

Untreated natural history: progresses from early localized (erythema migrans) → early disseminated (neuro/cardiac/migratory joint symptoms, weeks) → late disease (chronic oligoarticular arthritis in up to 60% of untreated patients; late neurologic/cardiac disease in < 15%).

Scanning EM — Borrelia burgdorferi, the corkscrew-shaped spirochete transmitted by Ixodes ticks
A nymphal Ixodes tick — poppy-seed sized and easy to miss on skin exam
Engorged tick after a prolonged blood meal — transmission risk rises sharply the longer a tick stays attached
LO 2 Clinical Presentation
Three-Stage Framework

Lyme disease classically unfolds in three (overlapping, not always sequential) stages. Mnemonic: think of someone making a FACE when biting into a "lime" — Facial nerve palsy, Arthritis, Carditis, Erythema migrans.

Stage I — Early Localized

Onset 7–14 days post-bite

  • Erythema migrans — expanding "bull's-eye" rash with central clearing at the bite site; warm, painless, ± pruritic; self-limited (resolves in 3–4 weeks)
  • Flu-like symptoms: fever, headache, fatigue/malaise, myalgia/arthralgia

Stage II — Early Disseminated

Onset 3–10 weeks post-bite

  • Fatigue, fever, flu-like sx; headache, stiff neck, myalgias, N/V, chronic fatigue; aseptic meningitis
  • Migratory arthralgia; multiple secondary EM lesions
  • Early neuroborreliosis — often bilateral facial palsy, radiculoneuritis/plexopathy, mononeuritis multiplex
  • Lyme carditis — fluctuating AV block, myopericarditis
  • Borrelial lymphocytoma (bluish-red nodule, ear/nipple/face — mainly European disease)

Stage III — Late / Persistent

Onset months–years post-bite, if untreated

  • Lyme arthritis — mono/oligoarthritis of large joints (esp. knee); occurs in up to 60% of untreated patients
  • Late neuroborreliosis (< 15% of untreated cases) — cognitive impairment, gait abnormality, bladder dysfunction, peripheral polyneuropathy; progressive encephalomyelitis is rare but severe
  • Acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (Europe/Asia only — B. afzelii)
  • Cranial or peripheral neuritis — facial palsy remains the single most frequent finding across all disseminated stages
Erythema migrans — expanding annular rash with central clearing ("bull's-eye")
Erythema migrans — close-up showing the central bite punctum
Borrelial lymphocytoma — bluish-red nodular swelling of the earlobe, a stage-II cutaneous finding
Red Flags / Coinfection Clues
  • PR prolongation > 300 ms, high-degree AV block, or symptomatic bradycardia → admit for cardiac monitoring
  • Encephalitis or myelitis (parenchymal CNS involvement) → IV therapy, not oral
  • High-grade fever, hemolytic anemia, or persistent systemic symptoms after the rash resolves → consider tick-borne coinfection (babesiosis, anaplasmosis)
Pearl

Bilateral facial (CN VII) palsy is a short differential: Lyme disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, sarcoidosis, and (rarely) bilateral parotid disease. Unilateral facial palsy in an endemic area during summer should still prompt a Lyme history — but bilaterality is the finding that should move Lyme to the top of the list over idiopathic Bell palsy.

LO 3 Diagnostic Workup
PresentationWorkupWhat it shows
Typical erythema migransClinical diagnosisNo serology needed — testing is unreliable this early (antibodies haven't developed yet)
Atypical rash or disseminated symptomsTwo-tier Lyme serologyScreen: ELISA or IFA (IgM/IgG) → if positive/equivocal, confirm with Western blot or 2nd-tier immunoassay
Suspected neuroborreliosisLumbar puncture (selected cases)Lymphocytic/monocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein; elevated CSF/serum antibody index supports active CNS infection
Suspected Lyme carditisECG, troponinFluctuating AV block (most common), other arrhythmias; troponin may be mildly elevated
Suspected Lyme arthritisArthrocentesisMainly to exclude septic arthritis; synovial WBC ~25,000/mm³ with > 50% neutrophils, culture-negative
Interpreting serology
  • IgM+/IgG−: consistent with acute/recent infection
  • IgG+: consistent with recent or remote infection — both IgM and IgG can persist for years after successful treatment
  • False positives occur with syphilis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, SLE, and rheumatoid arthritis
  • PCR/culture of CSF has low sensitivity for B. burgdorferi and is not recommended for neuroborreliosis
LO 4 Treatment
Antibiotic Therapy

Oral therapy (preferred where possible)

  • Doxycycline (oral tetracycline) — first-line for most presentations
  • Amoxicillin or cefuroxime axetil — alternatives, including in young children or pregnancy where doxycycline is avoided
  • Indicated for: erythema migrans, mild neuroborreliosis without parenchymal CNS involvement, mild carditis, Lyme arthritis

IV therapy (severe / CNS disease)

  • Ceftriaxone — preferred IV agent
  • Penicillin when indicated
  • Indicated for: encephalitis/myelitis (parenchymal CNS involvement), severe meningitis, severe carditis, treatment-refractory arthritis

Duration is presentation-dependent (roughly 14–28 days). For exact dosing and pediatric/pregnancy contraindications, see Shapiro 2014 (course reference) — dosages are deliberately not reproduced here since they weren't included in the source excerpt.

LO 5 Monitoring & Complications
What to track
  • Reinfection is possible — prior infection does not confer lasting immunity
  • Inadequately treated disease can progress to chronic/persistent infection with ongoing joint, neurologic, and cardiac manifestations
  • Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS): nonspecific pain, fatigue, and cognitive complaints lasting > 6 months after otherwise successful treatment. Pathophysiology is unknown; diagnosis requires excluding treatment failure and reinfection. Inflammatory markers are typically normal. There is no proven benefit to prolonged/repeat antibiotic courses — management is reassurance, education, and symptom-directed supportive care.
LO 6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Risk reduction
  • Avoid tick-infested areas (tall brush/grass in forests and fields); landscape modification around the home reduces exposure
  • Wear protective clothing (long sleeves/pants, light colors so ticks are easier to spot); use tick repellent/pesticides
  • Perform daily body checks after outdoor exposure; remove attached ticks promptly — grasp with forceps at the point of attachment and pull straight out with steady pressure. Avoid folk remedies (nail polish, petroleum jelly, heat) which can provoke the tick to inject more saliva
  • No vaccine is currently available for human use

Postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) can be considered when all of the following are met: the tick is an identified Ixodes species, the bite occurred in a highly endemic area, the tick was attached ≥ 36 hours, and prophylaxis (single-dose doxycycline) can start within 72 hours of tick removal.

🌡️ Varicella Zoster (VZV)

How boards would word it

"A 61-year-old woman presents with three days of severe right ear pain followed by new right-sided facial droop this morning. She cannot fully close her right eye and reports a metallic taste on the right side of her tongue. Examination reveals grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the right pinna and external auditory canal. She also notes decreased hearing on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) — VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion
What to look for: unilateral facial palsy plus ear pain, vesicles in the ear canal/pinna, and taste or hearing change localizes reactivation to the geniculate ganglion (CN VII/VIII). The vesicles are what separate this from idiopathic Bell palsy — and from Lyme-associated facial palsy, which is more often bilateral and non-vesicular.
▶
▶ Chickenpox and Shingles (Varicella-Zoster Virus)
Video — "Chickenpox and Shingles (Varicella-Zoster Virus)" (YouTube)
LO 1 Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

VZV is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family. Primary infection causes varicella (chickenpox); the virus then establishes lifelong latency in the dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia. Reactivation produces herpes zoster (shingles) — Gr./Lat. for "belt," describing the dermatomal band of rash. Herpes zoster is the most common viral infection of the peripheral nervous system.

  • Pre-vaccine era: ~4 million varicella cases/year in the US; > 95% seroprevalence by adulthood. Vaccination has cut incidence and associated morbidity/mortality by ≥ 88%
  • Herpes zoster affects > 1 million people/year in the US (~3–5 cases per 1,000 person-years); incidence has been rising over the past six decades
  • Lifetime risk of zoster is ~30% overall, up to ~50% in those who live to age 85; roughly 1/3 of people harboring latent VZV will eventually develop an episode
  • Transmission: airborne route and direct contact with vesicular fluid; household attack rate in susceptible contacts is ~80%

Risk factors for zoster: increasing age (the single most important factor), immunosuppression (HIV, transplant, lymphoma/leukemia, chronic corticosteroids, thiopurines, JAK inhibitors, anti-TNF agents — 20- to 100-fold increased risk), diabetes mellitus, cancer, female sex, white race, family history of zoster, and varicella infection before age 1 (predisposes to childhood zoster).

Pathophysiology

Primary varicella infection begins in the skin/respiratory mucosa; during primary viremia, VZV seeds multiple sensory ganglia, where latency is maintained by ongoing VZV-specific T-cell immunity. With aging or immunosuppression, declining cellular immunity permits reactivation: an acute inflammatory reaction develops in the affected ganglion, with ganglionic necrosis, neuron loss, and mononuclear infiltration. The virus then travels anterogradely along the sensory nerve to the corresponding dermatome, replicating in keratinocytes and producing the characteristic vesicular rash. Focal axonal loss follows ganglionic cell loss, and alpha-motoneuron loss has been reported in some cases — the basis for occasional zoster-associated motor weakness.

Primary VZV infection (skin/mucosa)
→
Viremia seeds dorsal root / cranial sensory ganglia
→
Lifelong latency (T-cell controlled)
→
Waning cellular immunity (age / immunosuppression)
→
Ganglionitis + neuronal necrosis
→
Anterograde spread along sensory nerve
→
Dermatomal vesicular rash (zoster)
Prognosis if untreated

Varicella is generally self-limited in immunocompetent children (resolves in 1–2 weeks), but complications — bacterial superinfection, pneumonitis, encephalitis — occur in 5–10% of cases and are more severe in neonates, adults, and immunocompromised patients. Neonatal varicella (maternal onset from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery) carried ~30% mortality before antiviral therapy.

Herpes zoster, untreated, resolves over 2–4 weeks but carries substantial risk of postherpetic neuralgia (~20% of patients), which can persist for months to years. Other untreated complications include vision loss (herpes zoster ophthalmicus), CNS vasculopathy/stroke, and motor neuropathy.

LO 2 Clinical Presentation

Primary Varicella (Chickenpox)

  • Incubation: 10–21 days (avg. 14)
  • Prodrome (1–2 days): malaise, low-grade fever, headache, anorexia
  • Rash starts on head/face and trunk, spreads to extremities; oral mucosa often involved
  • Hallmark: lesions at every stage simultaneously — macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → crust over ~24h per crop, with successive crops over 3–7 days ("starry sky")
  • 200–400 lesions typical if unvaccinated; breakthrough disease in vaccinated individuals is milder (< 50 lesions)

Herpes Zoster (Shingles)

  • Prodrome (2–3 days pre-rash): burning pain, paresthesias, or pruritus in a dermatomal distribution
  • Unilateral, confined to a single dermatome (most commonly thoracic); erythematous maculopapular rash → clear vesicles → cloudy → crust over 7–10 days
  • Radicular/burning pain, segmental sensory loss; occasionally delayed motor responses; lasts 1–4 weeks, typically involving 1–2 dermatomes
  • Special forms: HZ ophthalmicus (V1; Hutchinson sign on nasal tip → ocular involvement), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion: ear pain, facial palsy, taste loss, hearing changes), zoster sine herpete (pain without rash)
Varicella — diffuse rash with lesions at multiple stages simultaneously (the "starry sky" pattern)
Herpes zoster — grouped erythematous papules/vesicles confined to the T2–T3 dermatome, unilateral
Red Flags
  • Vesicles on the nasal tip (Hutchinson sign) in V1 zoster → high risk of ocular involvement, needs urgent ophthalmologic evaluation
  • Facial palsy + ear pain + ear canal/pinna vesicles → Ramsay Hunt syndrome, start antivirals promptly to reduce risk of permanent palsy
  • Rash spanning > 2–3 dermatomes or crossing the midline, especially in an immunocompromised patient → think disseminated zoster, evaluate for visceral involvement
  • New focal neurologic deficits weeks to months after a zoster episode → consider VZV-associated CNS vasculopathy/stroke
Pearl

Facial palsy differential by laterality and skin findings: bilateral, no vesicles → think Lyme disease, GBS, sarcoidosis. Unilateral with ear pain and vesicles → think Ramsay Hunt (VZV). Unilateral, acute, and otherwise isolated with no rash → idiopathic Bell palsy remains the leading diagnosis.

LO 3 Diagnostic Workup
PresentationTestNotes
Typical varicella or zosterClinical diagnosisSufficient in the vast majority of typical presentations — no testing needed
Atypical, prolonged, or non-responding; distinguishing from HSVVZV DNA PCR (preferred)Most sensitive/specific method (95–100%); vesicular fluid, scabs, blood, CSF, other fluids
Need a fast bedside answerDirect fluorescent antibody (DFA)Scraping from an unroofed vesicle base; ~3 hours but < 75% sensitive
Rarely used nowViral cultureUp to 14 days for cytopathic effect; largely replaced by PCR
Immunity status (not acute illness)VZV IgG serologyAcute/convalescent titers can help retrospectively
Suspected CNS involvementCSF PCR + anti-VZV CSF antibodies; MRIAnti-VZV CSF antibodies are the most reliable marker for vasculopathy; MRI shows ischemic lesions at gray-white junctions
Histopathology

Intraepidermal blistering, acantholysis, and multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions — indistinguishable from HSV without immunohistochemistry, which is why PCR is preferred whenever HSV must be excluded.

LO 4 Treatment
Antiviral Therapy

Primary varicella (HIV or complication risk)

  • Preferred: valacyclovir 1 g PO TID or famciclovir 500 mg PO TID × 5–7 days
  • Alternative: acyclovir 800 mg PO 5×/day
  • Severe/complicated: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h × 7–10 days, step down to oral after defervescence

Herpes zoster

  • Preferred: valacyclovir 1 g PO TID or famciclovir 500 mg PO TID × 7–10 days (better bioavailability/less frequent dosing than acyclovir)
  • Alternative: acyclovir 800 mg PO 5×/day
  • Start within 72h of rash onset — but still treat beyond 72h if new lesions or complications are present
  • IV acyclovir for immunocompromised/hospitalized patients or severe neurologic complications; foscarnet for acyclovir-resistant VZV

Acute pain management

  • Analgesics per the WHO pain ladder; opioids if severe
  • Gabapentin as an adjunct
  • Supportive skin care: drying agents, soothing lotions
  • Nerve blocks when indicated

Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN)

  • First-line: gabapentin, pregabalin, TCAs (nortriptyline, amitriptyline), topical 5% lidocaine patch
  • Second-line: topical capsaicin (0.075% cream or 8% patch)
  • Third-line: opioids
  • OMT is an emerging adjunct for refractory PHN pain — evidence is still limited and it isn't yet standard of care
LO 5 Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring during treatment
  • Track rash progression, new lesion formation, and pain severity at regular intervals
  • Monitor renal function with acyclovir/valacyclovir — dose adjustment needed in renal insufficiency
  • PHN pharmacotherapy: start oral agents at low doses, titrate gradually, watch for sedation, cognitive effects, and anticholinergic side effects, especially in elderly patients
  • Patients on opioids need monitoring for efficacy, side effects, and abuse potential
Long-term complications
  • Postherpetic neuralgia — most common complication (~20%); risk rises sharply with age; pain may persist months to years
  • Herpes zoster ophthalmicus — keratitis, anterior uveitis, glaucoma, cataracts, vision loss; patients with V1 zoster need ophthalmologic follow-up even after skin lesions heal, since stromal keratitis and uveitis can develop late
  • CNS vasculopathy/stroke — VZV infection of cerebral arteries can cause TIA, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, aneurysm, and dissection; risk is highest in the weeks to months after zoster but may persist beyond a year
  • Other neurologic complications: encephalitis, myelitis, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy, hearing loss), acute/progressive outer retinal necrosis
  • Recurrence: ~1%/year in immunocompetent adults over 50; 12–15% in the first year in people with HIV
LO 6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Vaccination — the cornerstone of prevention
  • Varicella vaccine (live-attenuated, Oka strain): children at 12–15 months and 4–6 years (2-dose series); susceptible adolescents/adults get 2 doses ≥ 4 weeks apart. Has reduced US varicella incidence by ≥ 88%
  • Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix): recommended for all adults ≥ 50 years, 2-dose series 2–6 months apart, regardless of prior varicella, prior zoster, or prior Zostavax. Efficacy > 90% against zoster and PHN; not a live vaccine, safe in immunosuppressed patients
  • Immunocompromised adults ≥ 19 years at increased HZ risk should also receive RZV (doses 1–2 months apart)

Infection control: patients with active varicella or zoster should avoid contact with susceptible individuals until all lesions have crusted. Postexposure prophylaxis with varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG) is indicated for high-risk susceptible contacts — neonates, immunocompromised individuals, and pregnant women.

🦠🖐️ Leprosy (Hansen Disease)

How boards would word it

"A 34-year-old man who emigrated from India two years ago presents with a several-month history of a hypopigmented patch on his forearm that he says feels 'numb to touch.' On exam, the lesion is a well-demarcated, dry, hairless plaque with a raised erythematous border, and he cannot distinguish sharp from dull touch within it. The ulnar nerve just proximal to the elbow is palpably enlarged and mildly tender. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Tuberculoid leprosy (Hansen disease)
What to look for: a hypopigmented, anesthetic skin lesion plus a palpably enlarged peripheral nerve is the classic diagnostic pairing for leprosy — two of its three cardinal findings. The small number of well-defined lesions with a distinct raised border (rather than numerous poorly-defined ones) points toward the tuberculoid end of the spectrum, where strong cell-mediated immunity localizes the disease.
▶
▶ Leprosy (Hansen Disease) — Mycobacterium leprae — Microbiology & Infectious Diseases
Video — "Leprosy (Hansen Disease) - Mycobacterium leprae - Microbiology & Infectious Diseases" (YouTube)
LO 1 Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

Leprosy (Hansen disease) is a chronic infection of the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes caused by prolonged exposure to Mycobacterium leprae — an obligate intracellular, acid-fast bacillus that cannot be cultured in vitro and thrives in cool tissue temperatures. It is one of the most common infectious causes of neuropathy worldwide.

  • > 200,000 new cases/year reported across ~150 countries (2019); ~80% concentrated in Brazil, India, and Indonesia. Rare in the US (~150 new cases/year); worldwide prevalence ~0.2/10,000
  • Peak incidence: ages 10–15 and 30–65; male > female
  • Incubation period is long: roughly 2–10 years (average estimates cluster around 3–5 years)
  • Transmission is mainly via respiratory droplets with prolonged close contact; transmission through skin lesions/contaminated soil is also possible. Household attack requires sustained exposure — casual contact is low-risk
  • Reservoirs: infected humans, and the nine-banded armadillo in the southern US (rare zoonotic transmission also reported from mangabey monkeys and environmental sources like sphagnum moss)
Pathophysiology

M. leprae preferentially infects Schwann cells of peripheral nerves and thrives at the body's cooler sites — skin, peripheral nerves, the anterior chamber of the eye, the upper respiratory tract, and the testes — which explains its characteristic distal, facial, and superficial-nerve distribution. Infection produces endoneurial fibrosis and multilayered thickening of the perineurial sheath, so nerve trunks become studded with palpable swellings, alongside chronic granulomatous inflammation of skin and nerve.

Where a given case falls on the clinical spectrum is determined by the host's cell-mediated immune response:

Lepromatous leprosy (LL)

  • ↑ Th2 response, reciprocally suppressing Th1 → weak cell-mediated immunity → many organisms (multibacillary)
  • ↑ Antibody production → hypergammaglobulinemia
  • Nerve damage results from direct bacterial invasion of Schwann cells
  • Poor CMI → more disseminated, more disfiguring, and the infectious/communicable form

Tuberculoid leprosy (TT)

  • ↑ Th1 response → strong cell-mediated immunity → granuloma formation (epithelioid cells + lymphocytes), few or no organisms (paucibacillary)
  • Nerve damage results from the T-cell mediated immune response itself, not direct invasion
  • Stable, localized disease
Prolonged M. leprae exposure
→
Dissemination to cool body sites
→
Schwann cell infection
→
Host CMI sets spectrum position (Th1 vs Th2)
→
Endoneurial fibrosis + perineurial thickening
→
Palpable nerve trunk swelling
→
Sensory / motor / autonomic deficits

A third pattern, mid-borderline (BB) leprosy, is immunologically unstable and sits between the two poles — numerous but poorly-defined lesions, sensory loss less severe than LL, but it produces the most numerous neuropathies of any form.

Prognosis if untreated: leprosy is slowly progressive; long-standing, untreated disease classically produces visible deformity from motor-nerve-palsy contractures and repeated unnoticed injury secondary to sensory loss (e.g., claw hand, foot drop, digit resorption).

Classification systems

WHO classification (by lesion count): Paucibacillary — ≤ 5 cutaneous lesions. Multibacillary — > 5 cutaneous lesions.

WHO disability grading — Hands/feet: Grade 0 (no anesthesia, no visible impairment), Grade 1 (anesthesia, no visible impairment), Grade 2 (anesthesia + visible impairment). Eyes: Grade 0 (no leprosy-related eye problems), Grade 1 (eye involvement, no visual loss), Grade 2 (severe visual impairment).

Ridley-Jopling classification — a clinical/immunologic spectrum from tuberculoid (TT) through mid-borderline (BB) to lepromatous (LL), mirroring the Th1 (TT) → Th2 (LL) immune gradient described above.

LO 2 Clinical Presentation
The three cardinal manifestations

Hypopigmented skin lesions, nerve thickening, and peripheral nerve palsies — this triad is the core of the clinical picture regardless of where a case falls on the spectrum.

Tuberculoid (TT) leprosy

  • Few (usually 1–3), localized, hypopigmented macules/plaques/papules with well-defined, raised, erythematous margins; dry, scaly, anhidrotic; overlying hair loss
  • Hyperesthesia of the lesion is common and occurs early (hypoesthesia develops only in later stages)
  • Nerve involvement occurs early but is localized — asymmetric enlargement of one or a few nerves; acute neuritis does not occur
  • Stable condition, good host cell-mediated immunity

Lepromatous (LL) leprosy

  • Multiple, symmetric macules/plaques/nodules with generalized skin involvement; facial nodules can coalesce into leonine facies; nodules may ulcerate; supraciliary/ciliary madarosis (eyebrow/eyelash loss)
  • Hypesthesia of lesions is less common and occurs only late
  • Nerve involvement occurs late but is extensive — acral, distal, symmetric anesthesia in a stocking-glove pattern spreading proximally
  • Early prodrome: nasal stuffiness, epistaxis; also hepatomegaly, nontender lymphadenopathy
  • Poor host cell-mediated immunity → more disseminated, more disfiguring, and the more communicable form
Leonine facies — thickened, furrowed facial skin with coalescing nodular plaques and madarosis, characteristic of lepromatous leprosy
Neurological presentation

Leprosy typically presents as a mononeuropathy multiplex affecting the coolest regions of the body, with thickened nerves often palpable through the skin. The most commonly involved nerves are the ulnar, common fibular (peroneal), superficial radial, posterior auricular, posterior tibial, and cranial nerves V and VII. Findings include weakness and atrophy plus loss of cutaneous sensation — especially thermal sense, often the first modality affected.

  • Ulnar nerve palsy: clawing of the 4th and 5th fingers, wasting of the dorsal interossei, sensory loss
  • Peroneal (fibular) nerve palsy: foot drop
Hand deformity in longstanding leprosy — digit loss at the IP joints, ulceration, and claw-hand positioning from ulnar nerve involvement
Pearl

Lepromatous leprosy manifests with Leonine facies; the Low cell-mediated immunity in this form makes it more Lethal in the sense of being more Leprosy-communicable (multibacillary, actively shedding organisms) — four L's worth remembering together.

LO 3 Diagnostic Workup
TestWhat it showsLL vs. TT
Skin scraping / slit-skin smear (modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain)Screens for acid-fast bacilli from skin lesions, nasal swabs, or earlobe smearsLL: positive at any site. TT: negative at all sites (paucibacillary)
Punch biopsy + histopathology (modified ZN stain, PCR)Confirms the diagnosisLL: foamy histiocytes packed with numerous bacilli, few lymphocytes. TT: granulomas with epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells, many lymphocytes (CD4:CD8 ~1.2:1), no bacilli
Lepromin testIntradermal antigen injected on the ventral forearm; positive if induration > 5 mm. Measures ability to mount a T-cell response — does not itself diagnose leprosy (can be positive without any leprosy exposure)LL: negative (poor CMI). TT: positive (strong CMI)
Serology (anti-phenolic glycolipid-1, PGL-1)Antibody test, most useful in lepromatous (multibacillary) diseaseMore often positive in LL
PCRConfirmatory testing of the biopsy sampleBoth forms, sensitivity higher in multibacillary disease
Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain — clusters of red-stained acid-fast bacilli (M. leprae) within tissue, high magnification
Diagnostic pitfall

The diffuse hypergammaglobulinemia seen in lepromatous leprosy can cause false-positive VDRL, RF, and ANA testing — a source of diagnostic confusion if the underlying leprosy isn't already on the differential.

🧬🦠 HIV & HIV-Associated Neuropathies

How boards would word it

"A 58-year-old man with HIV diagnosed 15 years ago, well-controlled on antiretroviral therapy, presents with progressive burning pain and numbness in both feet that has gradually crept up to mid-calf over the past year. He is tall and reports his symptoms are worse at night. Neurologic exam shows symmetrically diminished pinprick and vibration sense in a stocking distribution, with normal strength and preserved reflexes at the knees but absent ankle jerks. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: HIV-associated distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP)
What to look for: a symmetric, length-dependent, sensory-predominant pattern (stocking distribution, distal-to-proximal progression, preserved strength) in a patient with long-standing HIV is classic DSP. The "tall" detail isn't filler — height (longer axons) is an actual risk factor for this length-dependent process — and preserved strength with only ankle areflexia argues against a demyelinating process like GBS or CIDP.
LO 1 Natural History
Virology & Epidemiology

HIV is a retrovirus (family Retroviridae, genus Lentivirus) that targets CD4⁺ T lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. HIV-1 is the dominant species worldwide; HIV-2 is largely restricted to West Africa. Infection produces progressive immune dysfunction through CD4⁺ depletion and chronic immune activation; without antiretroviral therapy (ART), it typically progresses to AIDS.

  • US incidence peaks between ages 20–30 (~35/100,000 for HIV; AIDS peaks later, ~age 45, ~14/100,000); incidence is significantly higher in the Black population than other groups
  • Prevalence: ~1.2 million in the US; ~37 million worldwide
  • Transmission: sexual (~80% of infections worldwide — receptive anal intercourse carries the highest per-exposure risk); parenteral (blood transfusion highest risk, then needle-sharing, then needlestick injury); vertical (perinatal risk 15–45% without viral suppression, < 1% with suppression)
  • A viral load < 200 copies/mL makes sexual transmission essentially negligible ("undetectable = untransmittable")
  • Risk factors: men who have sex with men, injection drug use, a partner with HIV, multiple partners of unknown status, unprotected anal intercourse, and other STIs (genital mucosal damage from HSV/HPV increases transmission risk)
Pathophysiology — viral life cycle

The envelope glycoprotein gp120 (cleaved from gp160, encoded by env) binds the host CD4 receptor; fusion additionally requires a coreceptor — CCR5 (macrophages, and T cells early in infection) or CXCR4 (T cells, later in infection) — with gp41 mediating membrane fusion. Individuals homozygous for a CCR5 mutation have substantial resistance to infection; heterozygotes tend to have a slower disease course.

gp120 binds CD4
→
Coreceptor binding (CCR5 / CXCR4) + gp41-mediated fusion
→
Reverse transcriptase: RNA → dsDNA
→
Integrase inserts viral DNA into host genome
→
Replication, assembly, budding
→
CD4⁺ cell death + chronic immune activation

Natural course: explosive early replication in lymphoid tissue (lymph nodes, GALT) produces high viremia during acute infection — this precedes the window period (the gap between infection and detectable antibodies). Viral load then falls to a set point and remains relatively stable through clinical latency (~8–10 years), during which the virus continues replicating mainly within lymph nodes. Progressive CD4⁺ loss eventually impairs immune function, permitting the opportunistic infections and malignancies that define AIDS — usually the actual cause of death.

Prognosis if untreated: death occurs on average 8–10 years after infection, though this varies widely — some progress to advanced disease within a few years (median survival 12–18 months once advanced), while rare slow progressors remain asymptomatic for 20+ years. With adequate ART, life expectancy approaches that of the general population, though chronic comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer) remain more common.

HIV-Associated Peripheral Neuropathy — Natural History

Peripheral neuropathy is common in HIV: an estimated 20–40% of patients (roughly 1 in 6) develop some form, whether from HIV itself, a related opportunistic virus, or a toxic reaction to treatment.

Risk factors specific to HIV-associated neuropathy: HIV infection itself, older age, taller height (longer axonal distance — a length-dependent process), low CD4 count, and use of certain antiretroviral agents (some older NRTIs cause mitochondrial toxicity that produces a clinically identical peripheral neuropathy, which is exactly why distinguishing infection-related from treatment-related neuropathy can be difficult).

Emerging pathophysiology: increased plasma levels of miR-455-3p have been observed in patients with sensory distal symmetric polyneuropathy; this microRNA targets genes involved in maintaining peripheral nerve integrity, suggesting a possible mechanistic role in HIV-associated sensory neuropathy.

LO 2 Clinical Presentation
Staged HIV Presentation

There are no clinical features specific to HIV, and early infection is often asymptomatic (roughly half of infected individuals stay asymptomatic through acute infection). Incubation is typically 2–4 weeks.

  • Acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome): a mononucleosis-like illness — fever, fatigue, myalgia/arthralgia, headache, generalized nontender lymphadenopathy, generalized rash, GI symptoms (nausea, diarrhea, weight loss), oropharyngeal symptoms (sore throat, ulcerations, painful swallowing), occasionally aseptic meningitis
  • Clinical latency: may remain asymptomatic, or develop non-AIDS-defining conditions once CD4⁺ falls below ~500/mm³ — chronic subfebrile temperatures, persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, chronic diarrhea (> 1 month), oral candidiasis (scrapable white plaques), oral hairy leukoplakia (non-scrapable, lateral tongue, EBV-triggered), and skin findings like molluscum contagiosum, warts, or shingles
  • AIDS: defined by AIDS-defining conditions (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma) and/or a CD4⁺ count < 200 cells/mm³
Types of HIV-Associated Peripheral Neuropathy

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP)

Most common form, affecting up to 35% of the HIV population. Presents with numbness, burning, painful paresthesias, and prickling hyperalgesia in the distal extremities. Mechanism unclear — possibly related to treatment neurotoxicity as well as HIV itself.

Mononeuropathy multiplex

Painful, typically asymmetric; axonal degeneration with necrotizing vasculitis, seen mainly in AIDS-stage disease.

Progressive lumbosacral polyradiculopathy

Usually due to secondary CMV infection in AIDS patients; presents as a subacute inflammatory cauda equina syndrome (polyradiculitis) — bilateral leg weakness, saddle numbness, bowel/bladder dysfunction.

Inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy

Acute or chronic; resembles the more common non-HIV inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathies (GBS/CIDP-like pictures).

Less common forms include sensory ganglionopathy (rare sensory ganglionitis), autonomic neuropathy, cranial neuropathies, and an ALS-like motor neuropathy.

Red Flags
  • Subacute bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, or urinary retention in an AIDS patient → think CMV-associated progressive lumbosacral polyradiculopathy, a genuine neurologic emergency requiring prompt workup
  • Unexplained weight loss, depression, and/or dementia in a patient with a history of IV drug use → test for HIV
  • Esophageal candidiasis (unlike oral candidiasis) is an AIDS-defining condition
  • Any new or progressive neurologic deficit in advanced HIV should also prompt evaluation for opportunistic CNS/PNS infection, given the degree of immunosuppression
Pearl

Aerobic and progressive resistance exercise has evidence for improving pain scores in HIV-associated neuropathy — worth knowing as a genuinely evidence-based adjunct, distinct from pharmacologic management.
